ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability

Weiting Liu Affiliation: Fudan University Affiliation: JD.COM    Jieyi Bi Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University    Wanqi Zhou Affiliation: JD.COM    Jianfeng Feng Affiliation: Fudan University    Yining Ma Affiliation: MIT    Ai Han Affiliation: JD.COM    Wenlian Lu Affiliation: Fudan University
Abstract

Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

††footnotetext: †Project Leader.  🖂: Corresponding authors: Yining Ma (yiningma@mit.edu), Ai Han (hanai5@jd.com).

1 Introduction

Recent advances in tool-augmented agents have significantly broadened the real-world utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) Singh et al. (2025b); Jiang et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025b); Fan et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Fang et al. (2026). By integrating external tools into the reasoning loop, LLM-based agents have achieved strong performance across a wide spectrum of downstream tasks, spanning text-based question answering Wu et al. (2025b); Wei et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2025); Mialon et al. (2023), visual question answering Yang et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Zhang et al. (2026a), long-form text report generation Li et al. (2025e); Du et al. (2025a), and domain-grounded tool use Yao et al. (2024); Barres et al. (2025). Central to this progress are the ReAct paradigm Yao et al. (2022), which interleaves reasoning with tool invocation, and agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) methods Shao et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025a), which further refine tool-use capabilities via post-training. However, these successes largely assume a fixed, predefined toolset available throughout training. In practice, task requirements evolve continuously, often necessitating new tools such as web search for enhanced retrieval Jin et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025c), python interpreters for scientific computation Feng et al. (2025); Xue et al. (2025), file parsers for document understanding Team et al. (2025), and visual tools for multimodal perception Huang et al. (2026); Fan et al. (2026).

A natural question then arises: how can an existing agent efficiently adapt to an expanded toolset? The most straightforward approach is to directly apply agentic RL, allowing the agent to discover effective reasoning strategies and action policies via exploration. However, this strategy faces a fundamental difficulty. Since the agent’s policy has already converged during prior agentic RL training, it tends to fall back on familiar behavioral patterns, underutilizing newly introduced tools and repeating suboptimal reasoning strategies. This behavioral inertia leads to sparse rewards and inefficient exploration, as the agent rarely ventures beyond its established routines. An alternative is to rely on the tool-use generalization capability of the agent Zou et al. (2025); Du et al. (2025b), hoping that it can adapt to new tools without additional training. Yet, as our preliminary analysis in Section 3.3 reveals, generalization alone is insufficient. To better understand this bottleneck, we conduct a motivation study on failed student trajectories. A teacher model first identifies a decision round where an alternative local thought–action pair could plausibly redirect the subsequent rollout; we call this decision point a counterfactual anchor round (Section 3.2). The teacher then proposes this alternative using only the history before that round, yielding a teacher-revised context from which the student resumes generation. Compared with resuming from the original context, these teacher-revised contexts improve task success in both textual and visual search settings. This suggests that failures arise not only from limited tool-use capability, but also from missing contextual anchors that redirect reasoning and tool selection at key decision points.

In this work, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that bootstraps new tool-use capabilities through verified counterfactual context anchoring. ToolAnchor operates in three stages. In the Counterfactual Anchor hypothesis stage, diverse teacher models audit the student agent’s failed rollout trajectories and hypothesize anchor rounds where the agent’s decision deviated from a promising path. While the primary focus is on rounds where the agent failed to invoke a newly introduced tool, the teacher also considers suboptimal uses of existing tools and flawed reasoning steps, as these often compound the difficulty of adopting new tools effectively. For each identified anchor round, the teacher hypothesizes alternative reasoning and actions that would plausibly redirect the trajectory toward task completion. In the Counterfactual Anchor Verification stage, the student agent resumes generation from these teacher-anchored contexts under agentic rollout. Crucially, we retain for training only those anchor contexts that satisfy both verification criteria, namely task-level success and anchor-level usefulness, rather than accepting teacher hypotheses uncritically. In the Counterfactual Anchor Internalization stage, the verified contexts are used for agentic supervised fine-tuning (agentic SFT), allowing the agent to absorb the anchored behaviors into its own policy. This is followed by agentic RL, which realigns the internalized anchor behaviors with the agent’s previously learned agentic policy and supports robust, autonomous use of the expanded toolset.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We formalize the practical challenge of expanding a post-trained agent’s toolset. Through a motivation study, we identify behavioral inertia as the core bottleneck and reveal that counterfactual contextual anchoring at critical decision points can effectively redirect failed trajectories. (2) We propose ToolAnchor, a scalable, three-stage framework for capability expansion. It automates the discovery of counterfactual anchor rounds via diverse teacher models, strictly verifies their effectiveness through student rollouts, and internalizes these validated behaviors via agentic SFT and RL. (3) Extensive evaluations across general AI assistance (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) demonstrate that ToolAnchor seamlessly integrates new visual tools. Furthermore, it simultaneously boosts the base agent’s reasoning and existing tool mastery, offering a robust paradigm for continuous agentic evolution.

2 Related work

Tool-augmented deep research agents.

Deep research agents tackle open-ended question answering through long-horizon tool use: iteratively planning, invoking external tools, verifying evidence, performing intermediate reasoning, and synthesizing final answers Li et al. (2025b). This paradigm naturally encompasses general AI assistance, textual search, and visual search. Textual search remains the most extensively explored direction, where agents retrieve external evidence to answer complex queries. For instance, Search-R1 Jin et al. (2025), Search-o1 Li et al. (2025c), and WebThinker Li et al. (2025d) directly integrate web search into reasoning, while subsequent work advances this via agentic SFT and RL Wu et al. (2025a), systematic uncertainty reduction Li et al. (2025a), scalable data synthesis Qiao et al. (2025), dual-environment RL frameworks Li et al. (2025a), and continual pre-training Su et al. (2025). Building on these techniques, the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent Team et al. (2025) achieves competitive performance, and OpenSeeker Du et al. (2026) provides high-quality training datasets. Visual search extends this paradigm to queries requiring visual evidence, demanding agents to not only retrieve web pages but also understand and ground visual content in external knowledge. Benchmarks like VDR-Bench Zeng et al. (2026) and VisBrowse Zhang et al. (2026a) evaluate this capability, alongside VLM-driven agents such as T3-Agent Gao et al. (2024) and Vision-DeepResearch Huang et al. (2026) which explore multimodal tool integration. However, existing visual search approaches predominantly build agents from scratch with jointly designed toolsets, rather than extending well-trained text-oriented agents. This leaves a practical gap: given the immense cost of training capable deep research agents, incrementally augmenting them with visual tools is far more practical than starting over. We address this gap as a toolset expansion problem.

Agentic reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful post-training paradigm for LLM-based agents Zhang et al. (2025a); Yang and Thomason (2026); Zhang et al. (2026b). GRPO Shao et al. (2024) introduced group relative policy optimization for mathematical reasoning, and DAPO Yu et al. (2025) further enhanced its performance through a series of techniques. Although these methods can be applied to agentic RL settings, multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning introduces distinct challenges, such as distributional shift caused by tool feedback that deviates from the LLM’s training data. To mitigate these issues, several methods have been proposed: SimpleTIR Xue et al. (2025) filters trajectories containing void turns, GiGPO computes both episode-level and step-level relative advantages, and ARPO Dong et al. (2025b) and AEPO Dong et al. (2025a) use entropy-based adaptive beaming strategies to execute partial rollouts at high-entropy tokens. Despite these advances, existing agentic RL methods share a common assumption: the toolset is fixed throughout training. When new tools are introduced to a post-trained agent, its policy has already converged around the original toolsets, and standard agentic RL exploration mechanisms may be insufficient to overcome this behavioral inertia. Our work targets this setting through a teacher-guided anchoring mechanism that is then validated by student rollout. This design contrasts with standard knowledge distillation Hinton et al. (2015) and on-policy imitation methods such as DAgger Ross et al. (2011), which treat teacher-generated reasoning and actions as ground-truth supervision. Our framework treats teacher guidance as a hypothesis to be verified through student rollouts rather than as a direct supervised target.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Tool-use agent setup

Following Tongyi DeepResearch Agent Team et al. (2025), we consider a post-trained tool-use agent equipped with an original toolset UoldU_{\mathrm{old}}. In our experiments, UoldU_{\mathrm{old}} consists of web search, web browsing, a Python interpreter, scholar search, and a file parser. To study toolset expansion, we introduce a set of new visual tools UnewU_{\mathrm{new}}, including an image descriptor, a bounding-box extractor, and crop-and-image search. The resulting expanded toolset is U=Uold∪UnewU=U_{\mathrm{old}}\cup U_{\mathrm{new}}. Detailed tool descriptions are provided in Appendix C.1. We follow the ReAct framework, which consists of thought, action, and observation in each round. At each round, the agent first generates a thought and an action, and then receives an observation from the environment. This process forms a trajectory, denoted as ℋT\mathcal{H}_{T}, which is a sequence of thought–action–observation triplets: ℋT=(τ0,a0,o0,…,τi,ai,oi,…,τT,aT)\mathcal{H}_{T}=(\tau_{0},a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,\tau_{i},a_{i},o_{i},\ldots,\tau_{T},a_{T}), where aTa_{T} represents the final answer to the given question. For each non-terminal round t<Tt<T, the agent samples (τt,at)∼πθ(⋅∣ℋt−1)(\tau_{t},a_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}), after which the environment executes ata_{t} and returns oto_{t}. The terminal action aTa_{T} corresponds to the final answer, and no observation oTo_{T} is returned.

3.2 Counterfactual anchor contexts

While existing diagnostics (e.g., AgentErrorBench Zhang et al. (2025b)) focus on categorizing root-cause errors in failed trajectories, we move beyond passive diagnosis to active intervention. Specifically, we investigate whether replacing a single local decision under a shared history can redirect the rollout and recover a failed task. Aligning with recent advances in agentic context engineering Zhang et al. (2025b); Dou et al. (2026), this motivates our formulation of the counterfactual anchor context. Formally, given a failed trajectory ℋT\mathcal{H}_{T} and a non-terminal round t<Tt<T, the original local decision is the thought-action pair (τt,at)(\tau_{t},a_{t}) generated under history ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}. A counterfactual alternative retains ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1} unchanged but replaces this decision with a new pair (τt′,at′)(\tau^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t}), conditioned solely on the available information in ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}. The environment then executes at′a^{\prime}_{t} and returns the corresponding observation ot′o^{\prime}_{t}, yielding the counterfactual anchor context ct=(ℋt−1,τt′,at′,ot′)c_{t}=(\mathcal{H}_{t-1},\tau^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t},o^{\prime}_{t}). Crucially, ctc_{t} isolates the divergent branch: it captures the precise local context arising from the alternative decision (τt′,at′)(\tau^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t}) without altering prior history. We term ctc_{t} an anchor because it serves as a revised contextual reset point, rather than a full trajectory, from which the student agent resumes generation

3.3 Preliminary analysis

To investigate tool-use adaptation, we benchmark the text-oriented Tongyi DeepResearch Agent, extended with three new visual tools (image descriptor, bbox extractor, crop-and-image search), against two general-purpose models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct) on 100 random instances from VDR-Bench. As detailed in Table 1, the tool-call frequencies reveal a stark contrast: while general-purpose agents seamlessly adopt the visual tools, Tongyi remains heavily reliant on its original toolset. This discrepancy highlights a pronounced behavioral inertia in post-trained agents.

➤  Takeaway 1.  The tool-call statistics support the behavioral inertia hypothesis: under an expanded toolset, the post-trained student agent still relies disproportionately on the original tools and uses the newly introduced visual tools less frequently than general-purpose agents.

We further conduct motivation experiments on the textual search dataset OpenSeeker Du et al. (2026) and the visual search dataset VDR-Bench Huang et al. (2026). Specifically, we randomly sample 100 failed trajectories of the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent from OpenSeeker and VDR-Bench, respectively. For each failed trajectory, we use teacher models (Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5) to hypothesize the counterfactual anchor round and generate an alternative thought-action pair at that round (see Appendix B.2 for the prompt). We then have the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent resume generation from the teacher-revised context. Table 2 compares the task success rate when the agent continues from the original context versus the teacher-revised context. The results show that resuming generation from the teacher-revised context improves task success accuracy.

➤  Takeaway 2.  Teacher-hypothesized counterfactual anchor contexts can partially recover failed trajectories: compared with resuming from the original context, resuming from teacher-revised contexts yields higher task success in both textual and visual search settings.

These two findings motivate ToolAnchor, which systematically hypothesizes critical anchor rounds, verifies the counterfactual contexts, and internalizes the verified alternatives into the student agent.

4 Methodology

In this section, we present ToolAnchor, a framework for adapting a post-trained tool-use agent to an expanded toolset through counterfactual anchor contexts. ToolAnchor consists of three stages: counterfactual anchor context hypothesis, counterfactual anchor context verification, and counterfactual anchor context internalization.

4.1 Problem formulation

Building on the setup in Section 3.1, we study toolset expansion for a post-trained tool-use agent πθ\pi_{\theta}. The agent has been trained with the original toolset UoldU_{\mathrm{old}} and is then exposed to the expanded toolset U=Uold∪UnewU=U_{\mathrm{old}}\cup U_{\mathrm{new}}. The goal is to learn an updated policy πθ′\pi_{\theta^{\prime}} that improves task success under UU while preserving the agent’s existing capability on tasks solvable with UoldU_{\mathrm{old}}.

Our preliminary analysis in Section 3.3 reveals two key findings. First, the post-trained agent exhibits behavioral inertia, disproportionately relying on UoldU_{\mathrm{old}} even when UnewU_{\mathrm{new}} is available (Table 1). Second, failed trajectories can often be recovered when the agent resumes generation from a teacher-proposed counterfactual anchor context at a critical decision round (Table 2). These findings suggest that the bottleneck is not only missing tool-use capability, but also the lack of effective contextual anchors that redirect the agent away from its established behavioral patterns. This motivates ToolAnchor, which hypothesizes, verifies, and internalizes such contexts, as illustrated in Figure 2.

4.2 Counterfactual anchor context hypothesis

Given a failed trajectory ℋT\mathcal{H}_{T} produced by the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} under the expanded toolset UU, this stage uses teacher models to form a counterfactual anchor hypothesis. The hypothesis consists of a candidate anchor round t∗<Tt^{*}<T and an alternative thought-action pair (τt∗′,at∗′)(\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}}), which together define a revised context that may redirect the subsequent student rollout toward a successful trajectory.

Failed trajectory collection.

We first roll out the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} on the training datasets under the expanded toolset UU, collecting both successful and failed trajectories. We define the failed trajectory set as 𝒟fail={ℋT∣Success⁡(ℋT)=0}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fail}}=\{\mathcal{H}_{T}\mid\mathrm{Success}(\mathcal{H}_{T})=0\}, which serves as the input for the teacher-guided counterfactual anchor hypothesis.

Counterfactual round hypothesis.

We define an anchor round hypothesis as a candidate round at which an alternative local decision may induce a different subsequent rollout and potentially change the task outcome. Forming this hypothesis requires assessing how earlier decisions, observations, and subsequent reasoning steps interact across the trajectory, rather than relying on a fixed heuristic such as choosing the first or last suspicious step. We instantiate this step with a prompt-guided teacher audit: given the full failed trajectory, a teacher model sequentially reviews each round’s thought τt\tau_{t}, action ata_{t}, and observation oto_{t}, and selects a candidate anchor round t∗t^{*} where a revised context is likely to redirect the subsequent rollout. The prompt used in our implementation is provided in Appendix B.2. In our implementation, the teacher is instructed to use the following criteria:

  1. Criterion 1:

    Downstream impact. Prefer a round whose alternative local decision is likely to influence multiple subsequent steps in the trajectory.

  2. Criterion 2:

    Path redirection. Prefer a round that acts as a branching point, where a different local decision may redirect the subsequent rollout toward a different reasoning or tool-use path.

  3. Criterion 3:

    Strategic leverage. Prefer a round involving high-level agentic decisions, such as reasoning direction, tool selection, query formulation, evidence interpretation, information integration, or planning.

  4. Criterion 4:

    Counterfactual potential. Prefer a round where replacing the original local decision under the same history appears most likely to improve the final task outcome.

These criteria are intended to avoid trivial anchor-selection heuristics, such as always choosing the earliest suspicious step or the final decision step, both of which may fail to identify the round with the greatest potential to redirect the subsequent rollout.

Hypothesized context generation.

Once the anchor round t∗t^{*} is hypothesized, the teacher model generates the alternative thought-action pair in a separate step using only the history available before that round. Specifically, the teacher is given only ℋt∗−1\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1}, without access to subsequent rounds or the ground-truth answer. The teacher then proposes an alternative thought-action pair (τt∗′,at∗′)∼M(⋅∣ℋt∗−1)(\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}})\sim M(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1}), where MM denotes the teacher model.

This separation is important: the anchor-round hypothesis can use the full failed trajectory for diagnosis, whereas the alternative thought-action pair must be generated under the same information constraint faced by the agent at round t∗t^{*}. This prevents the alternative context from encoding future observations or the ground-truth answer, making the resulting supervision compatible with the student’s inference-time information state. Although new-tool adoption is a central motivation, the teacher is not restricted to rounds involving UnewU_{\mathrm{new}}. It may also select rounds involving ineffective use of UoldU_{\mathrm{old}}, or reasoning steps that make the subsequent rollout less effective. The environment then executes at∗′a^{\prime}_{t^{*}} and returns the corresponding observation ot∗′o^{\prime}_{t^{*}}. This produces the candidate anchor context c∗=(ℋt∗−1,τt∗′,at∗′,ot∗′)c^{*}=(\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1},\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}},o^{\prime}_{t^{*}}).

Teacher diversity.

A single teacher model may favor particular tool-use patterns or anchor-round choices when auditing failed trajectories. To improve coverage, we use a set of heterogeneous teacher models ℳ={Mj}j=1J\mathcal{M}=\{M_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J}, each of which independently forms counterfactual anchor hypotheses for the same failed trajectory. Different teachers may select different anchor rounds or propose different alternative thought-action pairs, yielding a diverse set of candidate anchor contexts 𝒟anchor={ci∗}i=1m\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{anchor}}=\{c_{i}^{*}\}_{i=1}^{m}. Each ci∗c_{i}^{*} is a teacher-hypothesized candidate counterfactual context and will be verified by student rollout in Section 4.3.

4.3 Counterfactual anchor context verification

Teacher-generated anchor contexts are hypotheses rather than ground-truth demonstrations. A teacher may select an ineffective anchor round, propose a plausible but unhelpful alternative decision, or generate an observation that does not support the student’s subsequent reasoning. To ensure data quality without manual annotation or heuristic reward shaping, we introduce a student-side verification stage. This stage retains an anchor context only when the student successfully solves the task after resuming from it and a separate judge model, with access to the completed trajectory, verifies that the anchor context was materially useful for the final success.

Anchor-conditioned agentic rollout and dual-level verification.

For each candidate anchor context c∗∈𝒟anchorc^{*}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{anchor}}, we let the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} resume generation from c∗c^{*} under the standard agentic rollout procedure, producing a complete trajectory ℋT′=Rollout⁡(πθ,c∗)\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T}=\mathrm{Rollout}(\pi_{\theta},c^{*}). We retain c∗c^{*} only if it passes two verification checks. First, the final answer in ℋT′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T} must be judged correct by the task-level evaluator, denoted as Jtask​(ℋT′)∈{0,1}J_{\mathrm{task}}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})\in\{0,1\}. Second, an anchor-level judge, denoted as Janchor​(c∗,ℋT′)∈{0,1}J_{\mathrm{anchor}}(c^{*},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})\in\{0,1\}, verifies from a global view that the proposed anchor context was materially useful in enabling the successful outcome. Formally, the verified effective-context dataset is

𝒟eff={(c∗,ℋT′)∣ℋT′=Rollout(πθ,c∗),Jtask(ℋT′)=1,Janchor(c∗,ℋT′)=1}.\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\{(c^{*},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})\mid\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T}=\mathrm{Rollout}(\pi_{\theta},c^{*}),J_{\mathrm{task}}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})=1,J_{\mathrm{anchor}}(c^{*},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})=1\}. (1)

Why verification matters.

Verification turns teacher hypotheses into training signals. The task-level success check filters out anchors from which the student cannot solve the task, and the anchor-level judge removes cases where success is not materially supported by the proposed anchor. Since the continuation after c∗c^{*} is generated by the student policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, the retained data avoid full teacher-trajectory imitation and remain closer to the student’s rollout distribution.

4.4 Counterfactual anchor context internalization

The final stage internalizes verified counterfactual anchor contexts into the agent’s policy through a two-step pipeline, combining local policy internalization and policy alignment with exploration.

Local policy update (anchor-only agentic SFT).

We perform anchor-only agentic SFT on the verified effective contexts, training the agent to reproduce the teacher-proposed thought-action pair at the verified counterfactual anchor round. For each verified counterfactual context (c∗,ℋT′)∈𝒟eff(c^{*},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eff}}, where c∗=(ℋt∗−1,τt∗′,at∗′,ot∗′)c^{*}=(\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1},\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}},o^{\prime}_{t^{*}}), the SFT loss is computed only on the alternative thought-action pair (τt∗′,at∗′)(\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}}), conditioned on the original history ℋt∗−1\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1}:

ℒSFT=−𝔼(c∗,ℋT′)∈𝒟eff​[log⁡πθ​(τt∗′,at∗′∣ℋt∗−1)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(c^{*},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{T})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau^{\prime}_{t^{*}},a^{\prime}_{t^{*}}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t^{*}-1})\right]. (2)

This objective directly injects the verified anchor behaviors at high-leverage decision points, providing a precise behavioral guidance. While optimizing solely on 𝒟eff\mathcal{D}_{\text{eff}} could risk localized overfitting, this anchor-only SFT serves as a targeted policy initialization. The subsequent post-SFT agentic RL stage then realigns these local updates with the agent’s prior broad capabilities, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting and preserving performance on tasks solvable with UoldU_{\text{old}}.

Policy realignment and exploration (post-SFT agentic RL).

Following agentic SFT, we apply agentic RL (GRPO) on the expanded toolset UU, using a binary task-level reward (1 for correct answers, 0 otherwise). This stage serves to integrate the internalized anchor behaviors from SFT with the agent’s prior RL policy, consolidating these local updates into a policy that is both aligned with prior knowledge and capable of effective inference under the expanded toolset. Simultaneously, it enables the agent to explore additional tool-use strategies beyond those explicitly provided by the teachers. Collectively, agentic SFT and agentic RL ensure that local counterfactual behaviors are internalized, properly aligned with the prior policy, and generalized, allowing the agent to leverage both newly introduced tools and previously learned capabilities.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental setup

Student and teacher models.

We use the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent Team et al. (2025) (Qwen3-30B-A3B) as our base model πθ\pi_{\theta}, which is trained via agentic RL on a fixed toolset UoldU_{\text{old}} consisting of web search, web browse, a Python interpreter, scholar search, and a file parser. We extend it with three visual tools UnewU_{\text{new}}: an image descriptor, a bbox extractor, and crop-and-image search. We choose the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent not only because its system prompts, toolsets, and model weights are open-source (allowing for training and customization), but also because it demonstrates strong performance on general AI assistant and textual search tasks. For the counterfactual anchor hypothesis, we employ Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5 as diverse teacher models to identify anchor rounds and generate alternative reasoning and actions.

Training datasets and benchmarks.

We use two training datasets that span both textual and visual search tasks: (1) OpenSeeker-1.5k, which contains 1,500 instances sampled from OpenSeeker-v1-Data Du et al. (2026); and (2) VDR-1.5k Huang et al. (2026), a visual search dataset that also contains 1,500 samples. We evaluate our method on three benchmarks corresponding to distinct tasks: GAIA Mialon et al. (2023) (General AI assistant, 165 samples), BrowseComp Wei et al. (2025) (Textual search, 200 samples subset following Du et al. (2026)), and VDR-Bench Zeng et al. (2026) (Visual search, test-mini split with 500 samples, following Huang et al. (2026)).

Evaluation metrics and baselines.

Following prior work Huang et al. (2026); Du et al. (2026), we adopt an LLM-as-a-judge approach for evaluation, using Qwen3-235B-A22B as the judge model. Specifically, we use the official prompts provided by each benchmark to assess the correctness of the agent’s final answer against the ground truth. Our primary evaluation metric is task success rate under Pass@1, where each query is evaluated with a single agent rollout. All benchmark results are reported with Pass@1. Pass@3 is used only during counterfactual anchor verification, where a candidate context passes task-level verification if at least one of three student rollouts solves the task. Please refer to Appendix B.4 for the corresponding evaluation prompts. We compare ToolAnchor against both proprietary and open-source deep research agents, including GPT-5 Singh et al. (2025a), Gemini-2.5-Pro Comanici et al. (2025), Claude-4-Sonnet, OpenAI DeepResearch, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking Bai et al. (2025), Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, OpenSeeker Du et al. (2026), Vision DeepResearch Huang et al. (2026), and Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al. (2025). Implementation details, including training hyperparameters, inference hyperparameters, and compute resources, are provided in Appendix C.2.

5.2 Main results

As shown in Table 3, we compare ToolAnchor-DeepResearch-30B-A3B against both proprietary and open-source deep research agents across three benchmarks.

Visual search.

On VDR-Bench, ToolAnchor achieves 28.8%, outperforming Gemini-2.5-Pro (18.8%), GPT-5 (20.4%), and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking (23.2%), despite using a smaller 30B LLM without prior visual-task training. This substantially narrows the gap with a vision-language model (VLM) agent trained from scratch for visual search, namely Vision-DeepResearch-30B-A3B (37.8%). This performance gap is a predictable trade-off: Vision-DeepResearch is a native vision-language model (VLM) agent jointly optimized from scratch on a 5×\times larger multimodal dataset (15K instances). In contrast, ToolAnchor operates on a frozen, text-only LLM backbone augmented purely via dynamic tool APIs. Achieving a competitive 28.8% without expensive multimodal alignment or massive data dependency underscores the remarkable parameter and compute efficiency of our toolset expansion paradigm.

General assistant and textual search.

On GAIA, ToolAnchor achieves 74.5%, improving over the base model (70.9%) by 3.6 percentage points and surpassing GPT-5 (67.4%), Claude-4-Sonnet (68.3%), and OpenAI DeepResearch (67.4%). On BrowseComp, ToolAnchor achieves 45.0%, a 1.6 percentage point improvement over the base model (43.4%). These results demonstrate that ToolAnchor enables the agent to acquire new visual tool-use capabilities while largely preserving its performance on the original textual tasks. The slight improvement observed on GAIA and BrowseComp suggests that internalizing effective counterfactual anchor contexts can also reinforce the agent’s existing tool usage and reasoning policies.

5.3 Ablation study

Visual tools.

Table 4 compares the baseline Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B model with a variant equipped with our visual tools. The results demonstrate that while the integration of these visual tools significantly boosts performance on the VDR-Bench visual search (from 7.5% to 16.6%), it incurs a marginal performance degradation on textual search benchmarks (GAIA and BrowseComp).

Post-training method.

Figure 3 ablates the post-training pipeline after visual-tool expansion. Agentic SFT on unverified counterfactual contexts performs poorly, especially on BrowseComp, indicating that teacher-hypothesized contexts can introduce noisy or ineffective supervision if applied without student-side verification. Using verified contexts improves over unverified agentic SFT on BrowseComp and VDR-Bench, supporting the utility of counterfactual anchor context verification. Agentic RL trained from scratch achieves moderate performance (70.3%, 41.5%, 21.6%), indicating that without access to counterfactual anchor contexts via SFT, RL alone exhibits limited exploration and fails to fully leverage the available toolset. However, agentic SFT with verified contexts alone still underperforms the ToolAnchor, suggesting that anchor-context internalization through SFT is insufficient to fully recover and improve the agent’s tool-use policy. By combining verified SFT with a subsequent agentic RL, ToolAnchor achieves the best performance across all three benchmarks. This indicates that verified counterfactual contexts provide effective local supervision, while the post-SFT RL stage aligns the internalized anchor behaviors with the agent’s previously learned policy.

5.4 Further analysis and discussions

Does the choice of anchor round matter?

To isolate the efficacy of our criterion-based anchor selection from the mere presence of teacher intervention, we benchmark it against three heuristic baselines: intervening at a random round, the first erroneous round, and the last erroneous round. Evaluated across 200 instances from both OpenSeeker and VDR-Train (using Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview as the teacher), our criterion-based strategy consistently yields the highest recovery rates. We repeat teacher anchor selection 50 times on one failed trajectory. As illustrated in Figure 5, effective anchors heavily cluster around strategic causal pivots rather than trivial first/last-error boundaries, confirming that a precise anchor location is as critical as the counterfactual context itself.

How many counterfactual contexts survive verification?

For each teacher-generated counterfactual context, we sample three student rollouts and use Pass@3 task-level verification, where a context passes if any rollout solves the task. We then apply anchor-level verification to successful rollouts, retaining only contexts whose success is judged materially attributable to the anchor intervention. Overall, 33.67% of candidates pass task-level verification and 31.98% remain after anchor-level verification, showing that verification filters noisy teacher hypotheses while retaining contexts that both recover the task and validly intervene on the failure point.

5.5 Case study

In Figure 1, we present a case study to illustrate how ToolAnchor redirects a failed visual-search trajectory. In this example, the base Tongyi DeepResearch Agent first uses visual tools to locate the green-hooded character and invoke the crop-and-image search tool, but then dismisses the returned visual-search leads as generic and switches to broad text search, eventually producing an incorrect answer. The teacher hypothesizes that this decision is the counterfactual anchor round, since it is the key point where the agent abandons the visual-evidence path. The generated counterfactual context instead keeps the agent on the visual-search path by analyzing the crop-and-image search results and issuing a targeted follow-up query. This qualitative example illustrates how a local counterfactual context can redirect the subsequent rollout. Details are provided in Appendix A. Consistent with this qualitative example, Appendix C.3 shows that hypothesized counterfactual anchor rounds are broadly distributed across different trajectory positions, with most occurring within the first 10-20 rounds, and that each can potentially produce distinct effects on the agent’s subsequent behavior.

6 Conclusion and limitation

In this paper, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework for extending post-trained tool-use agents with new tools through verified counterfactual context anchoring. Our main insight is that toolset expansion is not merely about adapting tool-selection and reasoning patterns to newly introduced tools. Post-trained agents may also need effective contextual anchors to break out of established reasoning and tool-use patterns. ToolAnchor turns teacher-hypothesized counterfactual contexts into training signals only after student-side verification, allowing the agent to internalize local high-leverage redirections rather than imitate full teacher trajectories. Experiments across general assistance, textual search, and visual search show that this mechanism improves new visual-tool use while also benefiting existing tool use and agentic reasoning, suggesting a practical path for capability expansion without retraining agents from scratch. In this work, the experiments rely on a limited set of teacher models and verified anchor contexts. Future research could investigate incorporating a more diverse set of teacher models and expanding the training dataset to enhance coverage, robustness, and generalization of internalized behaviors across a broader range of tasks and toolsets.

Appendix C ToolAnchor details

C.1 Tool descriptions

Web search

A web search tool that executes Google searches and retrieves the top 10 results. It accepts natural language queries and returns structured data, including page titles, URLs and snippets.

Web browse

A web browse tool (visit tool) that visits a specified URL and returns a summary. It accepts a target URL and a specific goal, uses Jina to convert the page content into Markdown, and then utilizes the DeepSeek-V3.2 summarization model to extract information relevant to the goal.

Python interpreter

A Python interpreter tool that executes Python code within a secure sandbox.

Scholar search

A scholar search tool that executes Google Scholar searches and retrieves the top 10 results. It accepts natural language queries and returns structured data, including page titles, URLs and snippets.

File parser

A file parser tool that analyzes various files and extracts their content as plain text. It accepts both local files and URLs, converting them into a readable text format for further use.

Image descriptor

An image description tool powered by the multimodal model Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. It supports both local image files and image URLs, and answers user queries about images.

Bbox extractor

A bounding box (bbox) extractor that uses the multimodal model Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to locate specific entities within an image. It accepts both local image files and URLs, as well as entity queries, and returns the bounding box coordinates of the requested entity.

Crop-and-image search

An image cropping and search tool that executes Google Lens and retrieves the top 10 results. It accepts an image as input and returns structured data, including titles, URLs, and snippets. The snippets are generated by the multimodal model Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, which compares the similarities and differences between the query image and the webpage images, a design motivated by VC-STaR Pan et al. (2026).

The Tongyi toolset includes a web search tool, a web browsing tool, a Python interpreter, a scholar search tool, and a file parser tool. The VDR toolset consists of a web search tool, a web browsing tool, a Python interpreter, and a visual search tool. Building on the Tongyi toolset, our toolset further incorporates an image description tool, a bounding-box extraction tool, and a crop-and-image-search tool.

C.3 Statistical analysis of counterfactual anchor rounds

Figure 6 shows the distribution of counterfactual anchor rounds hypothesized by Gemini-2.5-Pro on OpenSeeker-1.5k and VDR-1.5k. On both datasets, the hypothesized anchor rounds are heavily concentrated in the early stages of trajectories, with most anchors occurring within the first 10–20 rounds. This suggests that early counterfactual contexts exert greater influence on subsequent reasoning and tool-use decisions, while preserving sufficient rollout horizon for exploration and recovery. Similarly, on VDR-1.5k, the early-round concentration is even more pronounced, indicating that visual-search tasks particularly benefit from introducing visual-evidence-oriented contexts near the beginning of the trajectory. The long-tail of the distribution indicates that valuable counterfactual contexts also occur at later rounds in some trajectories. These observations support our use of teacher-guided anchor-round hypothesis generation rather than relying on fixed heuristics such as always selecting the first round.

Appendix D Data contamination

To mitigate search-time data contamination Han et al. (2025), we filter out specific domain names, such as github.com and huggingface.co, during the web search process.
